# Distribute through whoever already holds the customer

Source: https://lowob.com/research/distribute-through-whoever-already-holds-the-customer/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-17 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Fintech cannot buy its way to customers. Trust moves through partners who hold the relationship, practitioners who explain money, comparison and affiliate publishers, and owned channels. Paid goes last and small, because it is a reviewed category with low conversion rates, and the measures that matter are cost per funded account and retention, not sign-ups.

Fintech cannot buy its way to customers. Trust moves through partners who already hold the relationship, practitioners who explain money, comparison and affiliate publishers, and the company's own channels. Paid advertising goes last and small: it is a reviewed category, approval can take weeks and be withdrawn, and search benchmarks show finance converting below average. The only measures that matter are cost per funded account and whether the account is still funded at 30, 90 and 365 days.

## Paid is a reviewed category

Ad platforms treat financial products as a category needing review. You submit licensing, business documentation, sometimes the landing pages themselves. Approval can take weeks and can be withdrawn. Certain product types are restricted outright in certain markets.

The rules are specific and they move. Google's financial products and services policy requires verification in some locations, asks for licences and registration numbers, and requires the physical address and fees to be visible on the page. In June 2026 it extended verification to 24 more European markets, with rolling enforcement from 23 July 2026. Meta has required financial ads to US audiences to run in a special ad category since January 2025, with fixed age ranges, no gender targeting and no lookalike audiences.

When approved, you enter an auction shared with incumbent banks, large lenders and insurers. The incumbent next to you in the auction already has the trust you are trying to build.

The usual objection is cost per click, and the evidence is more nuanced than the folklore. WordStream's 2026 benchmarks, from 13,474 US search campaigns, put the average finance and insurance cost per click at $3.39, below the all-industry $5.42. The problem is what happens after the click: finance converted at 2.64%, and cost per lead was $74.44 against an all-industry $66.69. A lead is not a funded account, so the cost per funded account is higher again. Strangers clicking on a money product mostly do not convert, which is the trust problem in numbers.

So paid goes last, as in [Part 8](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/). In fintech, it goes last and small: retargeting people who already visited, and search terms that signal intent to switch. Everything else runs through the four channels below.

## Partners who hold the relationship

The customer already trusts someone with their money or their work. Employers run payroll. Accounting and payroll software holds the business's books. Marketplaces hold the seller's payouts. Community organisations hold membership and trust. Each of these can carry you to the customer inside a relationship that already exists.

This is embedded distribution, and it has a specific shape. It is slow to establish. Expect months of integration work, security review, and legal and compliance review on both sides. The partner's compliance team will read your claims register before their marketing team does.

It is also hard to revoke. Once a fintech is integrated into a payroll run or a marketplace payout, removing it costs the partner more than keeping it. Slow in, slow out. For a trust product, that is the trade you want. BCG's 2025 embedded finance research found US small-business adoption of vertical software reached 59% in 2024, described that software as a highly efficient distribution channel for embedded finance, and reported a 2.5 times lower attrition rate for embedded payments than for non-embedded.

Start with one partner who holds the segment you chose in [Part 7](https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-customers-are-design-partners/). Build the integration properly. Reference it in the next conversation. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to set the partner's role and payment before the first call.

> Slow in, slow out. For a trust product, that is the trade you want.

## Practitioners who explain

Between the product and the customer there is often a person who explains money for a living. Accountants for small businesses. Personal-finance creators for consumers. Newsletter authors for a specific profession. Bookkeepers, financial coaches, small-business advisers.

These people are trusted because they are independent. Pay them as if they will stay that way. The terms that work are cost per funded account, not cost per click or per sign-up. The practitioner is paid when the customer does the thing that matters, which aligns their advice with your outcome.

Brief them from the claims register. Give them the approved answers on safety, fees, protection and what happens when something goes wrong. Their audience will ask. If the practitioner improvises, the regulator will not blame only the practitioner.

The rules are explicit in the main markets. The UK Financial Conduct Authority's 2024 guidance on social media promotions says influencers who promote a regulated product without approval from an authorised firm may be committing a criminal offence; in 2024 it interviewed 20 finfluencers under caution. The US Federal Trade Commission's 2023 Endorsement Guides set out the potential liability of advertisers as well as endorsers, and require disclosure that is clear and conspicuous. [Referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers how to register, pay and disclose.

## Comparison and affiliate publishers

Comparison sites and affiliate publishers already rank for the question your customer is typing. They already answer it, and they already list your competitors. Not being there means the buyer sees the whole category except you.

Treat them as a channel with rules. They want accurate data on rates, fees and eligibility, kept current. They want a tracking link and a commission, which again should be per funded account. They want compliance-approved wording they can quote without their own legal review.

A listing on a comparison site is also a trust signal in its own right. The buyer reads it as "this product is established enough to be compared."

| Channel | What transfers the trust | Time to establish | How to pay |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Partners who hold the relationship | The partner's existing relationship | Months | Revenue share or per funded account |
| Practitioners who explain | Independence and expertise | Weeks | Per funded account |
| Comparison and affiliate publishers | Being listed beside incumbents | Weeks | Per funded account |
| Owned channels | Your own track record | Ongoing | Your time |
| Paid | None; it points at the others | Days to weeks to approve, if approved | Per click; low conversion |

## Owned channels and findable answers

Email, content and the product itself are the channels nobody can revoke. In fintech their main job is to hold the compliance-approved answers where buyers and answer engines can find them.

Every question from [Part 21](https://lowob.com/research/trust-is-the-product/)'s table gets a page: who is behind this, who holds the money, what happens when it goes wrong, what the fees are. Written plainly, approved once, kept current. Partners link to them. Practitioners quote them. Comparison sites pull from them. Answer engines ([Part 8](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/)) cite them.

The product is also a channel. A funded account that works well is the referral source every other channel is trying to imitate. Make it easy for a satisfied customer to send a friend, with approved wording and a tracked link, and check that referral incentives are lawful for the product and market.

## Measure funded accounts, not sign-ups

[Part 9](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) said stop reporting reach. In fintech, stop reporting sign-ups too. A sign-up that never funds is a verification cost and a data liability.

Measure cost per funded account by channel. Then measure whether the account is still funded at thirty, ninety and three hundred and sixty-five days, by channel. Practitioners and comparison sites will show you different retention than partners do. That difference tells you where to put the next quarter's effort. [From funded account to lifetime value](https://lowob.com/research/from-funded-account-to-lifetime-value/) covers the next step.

| Checklist item | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| Paid | Budgeted last, limited to retargeting and switch-intent search terms |
| Embedded partner | One partner who holds your chosen segment is in integration or live |
| Terms | Practitioner and affiliate terms set per funded account, not per click or sign-up |
| Briefs | Every practitioner and publisher brief carries the claims register answers on safety, fees and problems |
| Owned pages | A page exists for each trust question and is the source every channel links to |
| Reporting | Cost per funded account and retention at 30, 90 and 365 days, by channel |

## lowob takeaways

- **Put paid last and small.** It is reviewed, withdrawable and converts strangers poorly in finance.
- **Start with one partner who holds the segment.** Embedded distribution is slow to win and slow to lose.
- **Pay practitioners and publishers per funded account.** Brief them from the claims register; liability follows the firm.
- **Make owned pages the source of truth.** Partners, publishers and answer engines all draw on them.
- **Measure funded accounts and retention by channel.** Sign-ups that never fund are a cost.
